Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor

Empirical Asset Pricing Replication

Author

Taeheon Kim

Overview

Chapter 7 defines the sample that Part II of Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016) uses from here on: the monthly universe of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP. Before any predictive variable is studied, the chapter asks what this universe contains, decomposing it by stock exchange and by industry, in terms of both the number of stocks and their aggregate market value. It then defines the monthly stock return, explains how delistings are handled, and introduces the excess return that serves as the dependent variable in essentially every later analysis.

The second half of the chapter turns from individual stocks to the market as a whole. It chooses a proxy for the market portfolio, the Fama–French \(MKT\) factor, and examines its long-run reward and risk. Together, the sample definition, the return definition, and the market factor are the foundation on which the CAPM risk model and the cross-sectional analyses of the following chapters are built. This page follows the chapter’s own order and places the replicated figures and tables next to the book’s discussion.

1. The CRSP Sample

1.1 Sample Definition

For each month \(t\), the sample consists of every security in CRSP’s monthly stock names file whose name record is in force on the last day of the month and whose share code identifies a U.S.-based common stock:

\[ NAMEDT \leq \text{month-end of } t \leq NAMEENDT , \qquad SHRCD \in \{10, 11\} . \]

The first digit of SHRCD (1) marks an ordinary common share; the second digit (0 or 1) marks a firm incorporated in the United States. Exchange is not a condition: stocks on other exchanges, or with no exchange information, remain in the sample and are only separated out when the composition is examined.

The choice of the month-end rather than “any time during the month” is deliberate. Every analysis in Part II measures a predictive variable at the end of month \(t\) and relates it to the stock’s return in month \(t+1\). An investor deciding at the end of month \(t\) can only choose among the stocks that exist at that moment, so the sample is defined to coincide with that investment universe. A stock that was delisted mid-month is not available to that investor and is correctly excluded; a stock listed mid-month is available and is correctly included.

names = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ch07_msenames.parquet").filter(pl.col("shrcd").is_in([10, 11]))
names = names.with_columns(nd=to_date("namedt"), ne=to_date("nameendt").fill_null(date(9999, 12, 31)))

M0, M1 = 1925 * 12 + 11, 2012 * 12 + 11
sample = (
    names.with_columns(
        m0=pl.max_horizontal(midx(pl.col("nd")), M0),
        m1=pl.min_horizontal(midx(pl.col("ne")) - (pl.col("ne") != pl.col("ne").dt.month_end()).cast(pl.Int32), M1),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("m0") <= pl.col("m1"))
    .with_columns(m=pl.int_ranges("m0", pl.col("m1") + 1))
    .explode("m", empty_as_null=False)
    .with_columns(ym=((pl.col("m") // 12) * 100 + pl.col("m") % 12 + 1).cast(pl.Int32))
    .select("permno", "ym", "exchcd", "siccd")
)

The implementation expands each valid CRSP name interval into the month-end observations it covers. A name record starting on NAMEDT first covers the end of that same month; it last covers the end of the month of NAMEENDT only if NAMEENDT falls on that month’s final day, and otherwise the preceding month-end. Name records for one PERMNO never overlap, so each stock appears at most once per month, which the script verifies.

2. Composition of the CRSP Sample

The book decomposes the sample along two dimensions, stock exchange and industry, and along each dimension looks at two quantities: the number of stocks and their total market capitalization. The two quantities tell different stories. Counting stocks describes the breadth of the universe; weighting by market value describes where the economic weight of the market lies.

2.1 Market Capitalization

\[ MktCap_{i,t} = \frac{\lvert ALTPRC_{i,t} \times SHROUT_{i,t} \rvert}{1000} \]

SHROUT is the number of shares outstanding in thousands and ALTPRC the month-end price, so the ratio is in millions of dollars. ALTPRC is used rather than PRC because PRC is missing or zero when a stock neither trades nor is quoted on the last trading day, whereas ALTPRC falls back to the last available price. When there is no trade, CRSP stores the bid–ask midpoint with a negative sign, which the absolute value removes. If either field is missing, market capitalization is missing. Figures 7.2 and 7.4 report values in billions of CPI-adjusted December 2012 dollars.

    .with_columns(mktcap=(pl.col("altprc") * pl.col("shrout")).abs() / 1000)
base = cpi.filter(pl.col("ym") == END)["cpi"][0]
sample = (
    sample.join(msf, on=["permno", "ym"], how="left")
    .join(cpi, on="ym", how="left")
    .with_columns(mktcap_r=pl.col("mktcap") * base / pl.col("cpi"))
)

The first line is the book’s definition; the second block rescales each month’s value by the ratio of the December 2012 CPI to that month’s CPI, so that a dollar of market value in 1926 and in 2012 carry the same purchasing power. Without this adjustment the early part of the sample would be invisible on a chart dominated by recent nominal values.

2.2 Composition by Exchange

Group EXCHCD
NYSE 1 or 31
AMEX 2 or 32
NASDAQ 3 or 33
Other all remaining codes (regional exchanges, OTC, halted or suspended, no information)

Figure 7.1 — Number of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Exchange

For its first four decades the CRSP universe is essentially the NYSE. The sample grows slowly from about five hundred stocks in December 1925 to a little over a thousand by mid-1962, nearly all of them NYSE-listed. The series then shows two discontinuities that have nothing to do with the economy and everything to do with database coverage. In July 1962 AMEX stocks enter the CRSP file and the count jumps by roughly 800 in one month. In December 1972 NASDAQ stocks enter, and the count roughly doubles again. From there the universe expands through the 1980s and 1990s, peaks in November 1997 at about 7,500 stocks, and then contracts steadily; by December 2012 the sample has fallen by roughly half, to 3,742 stocks in the replication.

The July 1962 break explains a convention that runs through the entire empirical literature. Many predictive variables need one year of prior data, so the first month in which AMEX stocks can be used is June 1963. This is why most studies, and Part II of the book from Section 7.2.1 onward, begin their sample in June 1963 (return months from July 1963).

Figure 7.2 — Value of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Exchange

The number of listed stocks and their economic importance are not the same thing. The AMEX inclusion of July 1962 raised the stock count by about three-quarters, but the aggregate market value of the sample rose by only a few percent: the newly added stocks were numerous and small. The same holds for NASDAQ in December 1972, when more than half of the stocks in the sample but only about 13% of its value were NASDAQ-listed.

Historically, the value of the CRSP universe has been NYSE value. NASDAQ’s share becomes substantial only from the 1990s and peaks during the dot-com period, when it approaches 36% of the total in March 2000, the month in which the sample’s total real value also peaks. AMEX and the Other group never account for a meaningful share of market value at any point in the sample.

2.3 Composition by Industry

Stocks are assigned to broad industries using the SICCD field in CRSP’s monthly stock names file, grouped into the primary SIC divisions listed in Table 7.1. A SICCD of zero is not a valid industry code and is shown as “Missing”.

IND = [
    (1, 999, "Agriculture, forestry, and fishing"),
    (1000, 1499, "Mining"),
    (1500, 1799, "Construction"),
    (2000, 3999, "Manufacturing"),
    (4000, 4999, "Transportation, communications, electric, gas, and sanitary services"),
    (5000, 5199, "Wholesale trade"),
    (5200, 5999, "Retail trade"),
    (6000, 6799, "Finance, insurance, and real estate"),
    (7000, 8999, "Services"),

]
IND = [(lo, hi, full.split(",")[0].split(" ")[0], full) for lo, hi, full in IND]
IND_COLS = [short for _, _, short, _ in IND] + ["Missing"]
ind = pl.lit("Missing")
for lo, hi, name, _ in reversed(IND):
    ind = pl.when(pl.col("siccd").is_between(lo, hi)).then(pl.lit(name)).otherwise(ind)
sample = sample.with_columns(exch=exch, ind=ind)

The list is Table 7.1 verbatim, and the loop builds one nested when/then expression from it, so every stock-month receives the division whose range contains its SICCD and “Missing” otherwise. The book states the rule for zero; SIC codes that fall between the divisions (for example 1800–1999) have no book rule and are also placed in “Missing”, an implementation choice that affects very few observations.

Figure 7.3 — Number of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Industry

Manufacturing firms are the largest group in every month of the sample, and in the early decades they are the majority: the book reports that their share peaks above two-thirds in June 1946, which the replication reproduces exactly (583 of 864 stocks). The later sample looks different in kind. From the 1980s on, finance and services grow into the second and third largest groups, and by the late 1990s the two combined approach the manufacturing count.

The December 1972 jumps in several industries are not economic events. They are the NASDAQ coverage expansion of Figure 7.1 seen through the industry lens: the newly added NASDAQ firms were concentrated in finance and in firms without a usable industry code. The book reports that agriculture jumps from 87 to 810 stocks and finance from 247 to 748 in that month. The replication reproduces the finance count exactly, but the agriculture jump does not appear; instead the “Missing” group jumps to 719 stocks. This is consistent with placeholder SIC codes in the book’s data vintage having since been reset to zero, though the book gives no detail that would confirm the mechanism. The lesson for sample-composition work is the same either way: a break in an industry series should be checked against database coverage before it is read as a change in the economy.

Figure 7.4 — Value of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Industry

Figure 7.3 counts firms, whereas Figure 7.4 weights their economic importance by market value. On this measure manufacturing is even more dominant than by count, and the picture is more stable: the entry of many small NASDAQ firms in 1972 barely registers in value terms. Finance becomes the clear second industry by value only in the 2000s, later than it does by count, because many of the financial firms added in the 1970s and 1980s were small.

The dot-com period is where the value and count pictures diverge most. The transportation division, which includes communications, and the services division, which includes software and internet firms, rise sharply in real value through the late 1990s and give most of it back after March 2000. The same reversal is visible in finance around 2008. These are the industry components of the market-wide drawdowns that Section 5 examines.

3. Stock Returns and Excess Returns

3.1 Monthly Stock Returns

The monthly return is the RET field of CRSP’s monthly stock file: the return from the last trade of the previous month to the last trade of the current month, including distributions. For the vast majority of stock-months this is the return an investor would have realized, and it is used unchanged. The exception is the month in which a stock is delisted. The last trade price recorded in that month is not necessarily the value the investor ends up with, because the investor is typically still holding the stock when it leaves the exchange.

3.2 Delisting Adjustment

Delistings are often unexpected and leave no time to trade out of the position, so a return series that stops at the last exchange trade would overstate what investors earned, particularly for stocks removed for financial distress. CRSP’s delisting file records the delisting date (DLSTDT), a reason code (DLSTCD), and, when CRSP can determine a post-delisting value, the delisting return (DLRET). When DLRET is missing the book follows Shumway (1997) and imputes a return from the reason code:

Month \(t+1\) Return used
No delisting CRSP RET
Delisting, DLRET available DLRET
Delisting, DLRET missing, DLSTCD in {500, 520, 551–573, 574, 580, 584} −30%
Delisting, DLRET missing, other DLSTCD −100%

These are the specific delisting codes for which the book assigns a −30% return when DLRET is unavailable. They are not a single category: the list includes codes for a price below the exchange minimum, insufficient capital or float, and bankruptcy, but also for a move to over-the-counter trading, delisting at the company’s request, liquidation, going private, and “reason unavailable”. All other codes receive −100%.

ImportantReplacement, not compounding

The book “take[s] the return of the stock to be the delisting return.” In a delisting month the delisting return replaces the month’s return; it is not compounded with RET as \((1+RET)(1+DLRET)-1\).

BAD = pl.col("dlstcd").is_in([500, 520, 574, 580, 584]) | pl.col("dlstcd").is_between(551, 573)
dl = (
    pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ch07_msedelist.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("dlstcd") > 199)
    .with_columns(ym=ym_of(to_date("dlstdt")))
    .with_columns(
        dlfill=pl.when(pl.col("dlret").is_not_null()).then(pl.col("dlret"))
               .when(BAD).then(-0.30).otherwise(-1.00),
        how=pl.when(pl.col("dlret").is_not_null()).then(pl.lit("dlret"))
            .when(BAD).then(pl.lit("-30%")).otherwise(pl.lit("-100%")),
    )
    .select("permno", "ym", "dlstcd", "dlret", "dlfill", "how")
)

BAD is the book’s list of −30% codes. For each delisting event the code produces dlfill, the return that will be used in the delisting month: DLRET when CRSP has one, and the imputed value otherwise. The adjusted return is then obtained by taking dlfill where it exists and RET elsewhere, which is the coalesce in the next code block. The filter on DLSTCD is an implementation choice, not a Chapter 7 rule: CRSP’s codes in the 100s denote securities that are still active rather than delisted.

3.3 Excess Returns and Timing

Four return variables are used in Tables 7.2 and 7.3. With \(RF_{t+1}\) the monthly return on the risk-free security from Kenneth French’s data library,

\[ \begin{aligned} RET_{i,t+1} &: \text{CRSP } RET \text{, unadjusted} & ret_{i,t+1} &= RET_{i,t+1} - RF_{t+1} \\ R_{i,t+1} &: \text{delisting-adjusted return} & r_{i,t+1} &= R_{i,t+1} - RF_{t+1} \end{aligned} \]

all recorded in percent. The timing is the one described in Section 1.1:

end of month t          sample membership; predictive variables measured here
        ↓
month t+1               the stock's return, R_{i,t+1}, and excess return, r_{i,t+1}

Within one month’s cross section the same \(RF_{t+1}\) is subtracted from every stock, so raw and excess returns rank stocks identically and any cross-sectional pattern in one is a pattern in the other. The distinction matters in the time series: the risk-free rate varies over time, and a factor regression of returns rather than excess returns would let that variation contaminate the intercept. Since the intercept of such regressions is usually the object of interest, the book works with excess returns throughout, and \(r_{i,t+1}\) is the focal return variable of Part II.

panel = (
    sample.filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(T0, T1)).select("permno", "ym")
    .with_columns(ym1=ym_shift(pl.col("ym"), 1))
    .join(ret, left_on=["permno", "ym1"], right_on=["permno", "ym"], how="left")
    .join(dl, left_on=["permno", "ym1"], right_on=["permno", "ym"], how="left")
    .join(ff, left_on="ym1", right_on="ym", how="left")
    .with_columns(R=pl.coalesce("dlfill", "RET"))
    .with_columns(
        RET=pl.col("RET") * 100, R=pl.col("R") * 100,
        ret=(pl.col("RET") - pl.col("rf")) * 100, r=(pl.col("R") - pl.col("rf")) * 100,
    )
)

Each stock-month of the sample at \(t\) is given the key of the following month and joined left to the return, delisting, and risk-free tables at \(t+1\). The left join is what keeps the delisting adjustment meaningful: a stock that is in the sample at the end of \(t\) and delists during \(t+1\) stays in the cross section with its delisting return, whereas an inner join on the stocks alive at \(t+1\) would silently remove exactly the observations that Shumway’s adjustment exists to keep.

4. Return Distribution

Tables 7.2 and 7.3 summarize the cross-sectional distribution of the four return variables with the same two-step procedure used for the annual sample in Chapter 2, applied here month by month. Step 1 computes, for every month \(t\), the mean, standard deviation, skewness, excess kurtosis, minimum, 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles, maximum, and number of stocks with a valid value. Step 2 averages each of these monthly statistics over time. The reported \(n\) is therefore the average number of stocks per month, and every other entry is the time-series mean of a cross-sectional statistic, not a statistic of the pooled panel.

def xsec_m(df, var):
    c = pl.col(var)
    aggs = [c.mean().alias("Mean"), c.std().alias("SD"), c.skew().alias("Skew"), c.kurtosis().alias("Kurt"),
            c.min().alias("Min")]
    aggs += [c.quantile(q, "linear").alias(n) for q, n in zip(QS, ["5%", "25%", "Median", "75%", "95%"])]
    aggs += [c.max().alias("Max"), c.len().alias("n")]
    return df.filter(c.is_finite()).group_by("ym").agg(aggs).sort("ym")

def summary(t0, t1):
    d = panel.filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(t0, t1))
    months = pl.DataFrame({"ym": d["ym"].unique().sort()})
    rows, monthly = [], []
    for v in VARS:
        m = months.join(xsec_m(d, v), on="ym", how="left").with_columns(pl.col("n").fill_null(0))
        monthly.append(m.with_columns(var=pl.lit(v)))
        rows.append(m.drop("ym").mean().with_columns(var=pl.lit(v), n=pl.col("n").round(0).cast(pl.Int64)).select(["var"] + COLS_R))
    return pl.concat(rows), pl.concat(monthly).select(["var", "ym"] + COLS_R)

xsec_m() is Step 1 for one variable and summary() runs it for the four variables over a range of sample months and takes the Step 2 average. The only difference from Chapter 2 is the frequency: the unit of the cross section is the month rather than the year, and there are 1,038 of them.

Three features of the distribution carry over to everything that follows.

Positive skewness. In the average month the mean excess return is positive while the median is slightly negative, and the cross-sectional skewness is strongly positive. The asymmetry is structural: a stock cannot lose more than 100%, so the excess return is bounded below by roughly \(-100\% - RF\), but there is no corresponding bound above. A typical stock earns a little less than the risk-free rate in a typical month; the positive mean comes from a minority of large winners.

Fat tails. The average excess kurtosis is far above the value of zero that a normal distribution would give. The monthly cross section routinely contains returns of several hundred percent and of close to −100%, and the 5th and 95th percentiles sit at roughly ±20%. Any method that assumes normal returns, or that is sensitive to extreme values, has to contend with this.

Effect of the delisting adjustment. The adjusted and unadjusted distributions are similar in the middle: percentiles from the 5th to the 95th differ by hundredths of a percent. The adjustment acts in the tails. It lowers the mean slightly by adding many returns of −30% and −100%, makes the average minimum more negative, and, because some delisting returns are very large, raises the average maximum and with it the standard deviation and kurtosis. The book concludes that the choice rarely changes empirical results, but uses the adjusted return because it is closer to what an investor realizes.

In the replication the unadjusted rows (\(ret\), \(RET\)) reproduce the book to the second decimal on almost every statistic, and the adjusted rows reproduce the mean and every percentile from the 5th to the 95th. The adjusted standard deviation, kurtosis, and maximum are lower than the book’s. The discrepancy is thus concentrated in the delisting-adjusted tail statistics, and since the adjusted and unadjusted rows differ only in the delisting returns, delisting-return observations are the likely source. Confirming whether this reflects CRSP data-vintage revisions would require a record-level comparison with the book’s data vintage.

The post-1963 sample is a different universe rather than a shorter one. It contains on average about half again as many stocks per month, because the years with only NYSE coverage are gone and AMEX and NASDAQ stocks are present throughout. The inclusion of AMEX and NASDAQ materially changes the cross-sectional return distribution, which becomes wider and more heavy-tailed: the cross-sectional standard deviation, the skewness, the excess kurtosis, and the average maximum are all higher, and the average minimum is closer to −100%. The average excess return is somewhat lower and the median more negative. The distribution that later chapters work with is thus wider and heavier-tailed than the full-history one.

The comparison with the book follows the pattern of Table 7.2: unadjusted statistics match to the second decimal, adjusted percentiles and means match, and the adjusted dispersion measures are somewhat lower in the current data.

5. The Market Factor

5.1 Market Portfolio Proxy

In the CAPM the market portfolio is the value-weighted portfolio of all assets: stocks and bonds, but also real estate, private businesses, and human capital. That portfolio cannot be observed, and even the portfolio of all financial securities is beyond reach because many securities have no observable price. Empirical work therefore uses a proxy built from the securities traded on U.S. stock exchanges, whose prices are recorded every day.

The book compares two such proxies. The first is the value-weighted portfolio of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP, that is, of the sample defined in Section 1; its excess return is the Fama–French market factor, \(MKT\). The second is the broader CRSP value-weighted index, which also contains securities that are not U.S. common stocks (foreign-incorporated firms, closed-end funds, and other share types) but excludes ADRs. Over July 1926 to December 2012 the two excess-return series have nearly identical means and standard deviations and a correlation of about 0.9995. The choice between them is immaterial, and the book uses \(MKT\) as the market proxy for the remainder of the text.

5.2 Long-Run Market Performance

Statistic Book Replication Difference
"Mean monthly excess return (%)" 0.63 0.63 0.00
"Monthly standard deviation (%)" 5.43 5.45 0.02
"Annualized Sharpe ratio" 0.40 0.40 -0.00
"Compounded excess return, Jul … 14209.00 14410.79 201.79
"Cumulative log excess return (… 496.00 497.75 1.75

The annualized Sharpe ratio is the monthly mean over the monthly standard deviation times \(\sqrt{12}\), which assumes independent monthly returns. A premium of roughly 0.6% per month with a standard deviation of over 5% is a noisy reward: the market’s excess return in a single month is far more likely to be dominated by risk than by the premium, and the premium reveals itself only through compounding over decades.

5.3 Figure 7.5 — Cumulative Excess Returns of MKT

\[ \text{Compounded excess return}_t = 100 \times \Bigl[\prod_{s \le t}(1 + MKT_s) - 1\Bigr], \qquad \text{Cumulative log excess return}_t = 100 \times \sum_{s \le t} \ln(1 + MKT_s). \]

mkt = (
    ff.filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(192607, 201212)).sort("ym")
    .with_columns(logret=(1 + pl.col("mktrf")).log(), wealth=(1 + pl.col("mktrf")).cum_prod())
    .with_columns(
        compound_excess=100 * (pl.col("wealth") - 1),
        cumulative_log_excess=100 * pl.col("logret").cum_sum(),
        drawdown=pl.col("wealth") / pl.col("wealth").cum_max() - 1,
        date=pl.date(pl.col("ym") // 100, pl.col("ym") % 100, 1).dt.month_end(),
    )
)

The compounded series is the cumulative product of one plus the monthly market excess return, expressed as a percentage gain; the log series is the running sum of the log of one plus the monthly excess return. wealth is the cumulative product itself and is reused below for the drawdown calculation.

The two series contain the same information, plotted on scales that answer different questions. The compounded series gives the level: the compounded excess-return index grows to about 145 times its initial level by December 2012, corresponding to a cumulative excess return of about 14,411%. But because that number is a level, equal percentage moves are drawn as ever larger vertical distances as the index grows, so the solid line makes the late sample look far more volatile than the early one and makes the 1929–1932 crash, the largest percentage loss in the sample, almost invisible. The log series removes that distortion: a 10% loss is the same vertical distance in 1930 as in 2008, which is why the dashed line shows the early crash as the deep trough it was.

Major Drawdowns

Episode (peak → trough) Book drawdown Replication Book recovery Replication recovery
"1929-08 → 1932-06" "about -85%" "-84.6%" "1945-04" "1945-04"
"1968-11 → 1974-09" "about -56%" "-55.7%" "1983-04" "1983-04"
"1987-08 → 1987-11" "about -31%" "-31.0%" "1991-05" "1991-05"
"2000-03 → 2009-02" "about -54%" "-54.2%" "not by Dec 2012" "not by Dec 2012"

Drawdowns are measured from the running high-water mark of the compounded series; recovery is the first month in which cumulative wealth again reaches the previous peak. The 1929 crash needed more than fifteen years to recover; the 1968 and 2000 episodes, each more than half of cumulative wealth, needed fourteen years and more than the twelve years remaining in the sample, respectively. October 1987, with a monthly excess return of about −23%, produced the smallest of the four drawdowns and the fastest recovery.

Figure 7.5 shows that a strongly positive long-run market premium can coexist with very large and long-lasting drawdowns. The premium is real, but an investor collects it only by holding through periods in which more than half of accumulated wealth disappears and is not recovered for a decade or more. In the CAPM, beta measures a stock’s exposure to variation in this market factor.

Summary

Chapter 7 fixes the objects that the rest of the book takes as given. The sample is the set of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP at each month-end, whose composition by exchange and by industry changes materially over 1925–2012, both through real economic shifts and through discrete changes in database coverage in 1962 and 1972. The monthly return is CRSP’s RET with the delisting month replaced by the delisting return or its Shumway (1997) imputation, an adjustment that leaves the center of the cross-sectional distribution unchanged but matters in its tails. The one-month-ahead excess return \(r_{i,t+1}\) is the focal return variable, and its cross section is strongly right-skewed and heavy-tailed.

The market portfolio is proxied by the Fama–French \(MKT\) factor, whose long-run premium is unmistakably positive and yet is earned through drawdowns of 50–85% lasting a decade or more. Every asset-pricing analysis in the chapters that follow, from the CAPM risk model to the cross-sectional regressions of Part II, is built on this sample, these return definitions, and this market factor.

# Overview

Chapter 7 defines the sample that Part II of Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016)
uses from here on: the monthly universe of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP.
Before any predictive variable is studied, the chapter asks what this
universe contains, decomposing it by stock exchange and by industry, in
terms of both the number of stocks and their aggregate market value. It then
defines the monthly stock return, explains how delistings are handled, and
introduces the excess return that serves as the dependent variable in
essentially every later analysis.

The second half of the chapter turns from individual stocks to the market as
a whole. It chooses a proxy for the market portfolio, the Fama–French $MKT$
factor, and examines its long-run reward and risk. Together, the sample
definition, the return definition, and the market factor are the foundation
on which the CAPM risk model and the cross-sectional analyses of the
following chapters are built. This page follows the chapter's own order and
places the replicated figures and tables next to the book's discussion.

---

# 1. The CRSP Sample

## 1.1 Sample Definition

For each month $t$, the sample consists of every security in CRSP's monthly
stock names file whose name record is in force on the last day of the month
and whose share code identifies a U.S.-based common stock:

$$
NAMEDT \leq \text{month-end of } t \leq NAMEENDT ,
\qquad
SHRCD \in \{10, 11\} .
$$

The first digit of `SHRCD` (1) marks an ordinary common share; the second
digit (0 or 1) marks a firm incorporated in the United States. Exchange is
not a condition: stocks on other exchanges, or with no exchange information,
remain in the sample and are only separated out when the composition is
examined.

The choice of the *month-end* rather than "any time during the month" is
deliberate. Every analysis in Part II measures a predictive variable at the
end of month $t$ and relates it to the stock's return in month $t+1$. An
investor deciding at the end of month $t$ can only choose among the stocks
that exist at that moment, so the sample is defined to coincide with that
investment universe. A stock that was delisted mid-month is not available to
that investor and is correctly excluded; a stock listed mid-month is
available and is correctly included.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", 'names = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ch07_msenames.parquet")', "dup =")
```

The implementation expands each valid CRSP name interval into the month-end
observations it covers. A name record starting on `NAMEDT` first covers the
end of that same month; it last covers the end of the month of `NAMEENDT`
only if `NAMEENDT` falls on that month's final day, and otherwise the
preceding month-end. Name records for one `PERMNO` never overlap, so each
stock appears at most once per month, which the script verifies.

---

# 2. Composition of the CRSP Sample

The book decomposes the sample along two dimensions, stock exchange and
industry, and along each dimension looks at two quantities: the number of
stocks and their total market capitalization. The two quantities tell
different stories. Counting stocks describes the breadth of the universe;
weighting by market value describes where the economic weight of the market
lies.

## 2.1 Market Capitalization

$$
MktCap_{i,t} = \frac{\lvert ALTPRC_{i,t} \times SHROUT_{i,t} \rvert}{1000}
$$

`SHROUT` is the number of shares outstanding in thousands and `ALTPRC` the
month-end price, so the ratio is in millions of dollars. `ALTPRC` is used
rather than `PRC` because `PRC` is missing or zero when a stock neither
trades nor is quoted on the last trading day, whereas `ALTPRC` falls back to
the last available price. When there is no trade, CRSP stores the bid–ask
midpoint with a negative sign, which the absolute value removes. If either
field is missing, market capitalization is missing. Figures 7.2 and 7.4
report values in billions of CPI-adjusted December 2012 dollars.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", ".with_columns(mktcap=", '.select("permno", "ym", "mktcap")')
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", "base = cpi", 'print(f"MktCap')
```

The first line is the book's definition; the second block rescales each
month's value by the ratio of the December 2012 CPI to that month's CPI, so
that a dollar of market value in 1926 and in 2012 carry the same purchasing
power. Without this adjustment the early part of the sample would be
invisible on a chart dominated by recent nominal values.

## 2.2 Composition by Exchange

| Group | `EXCHCD` |
|---|---|
| NYSE | 1 or 31 |
| AMEX | 2 or 32 |
| NASDAQ | 3 or 33 |
| Other | all remaining codes (regional exchanges, OTC, halted or suspended, no information) |

### Figure 7.1 — Number of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Exchange

![](../output/figures/fig71_n_exch.png)

For its first four decades the CRSP universe is essentially the NYSE. The
sample grows slowly from about five hundred stocks in December 1925 to a
little over a thousand by mid-1962, nearly all of them NYSE-listed. The
series then shows two discontinuities that have nothing to do with the
economy and everything to do with database coverage. In July 1962 AMEX
stocks enter the CRSP file and the count jumps by roughly 800 in one month.
In December 1972 NASDAQ stocks enter, and the count roughly doubles again.
From there the universe expands through the 1980s and 1990s, peaks in
November 1997 at about 7,500 stocks, and then contracts steadily; by
December 2012 the sample has fallen by roughly half, to
`{python} f"{at(n_exch, 201212)['Total']:,}"` stocks in the replication.

The July 1962 break explains a convention that runs through the entire
empirical literature. Many predictive variables need one year of prior data,
so the first month in which AMEX stocks can be used is June 1963. This is why
most studies, and Part II of the book from Section 7.2.1 onward, begin their
sample in June 1963 (return months from July 1963).

### Figure 7.2 — Value of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Exchange

![](../output/figures/fig72_cap_exch.png)

The number of listed stocks and their economic importance are not the same
thing. The AMEX inclusion of July 1962 raised the stock count by about
three-quarters, but the aggregate market value of the sample rose by only a
few percent: the newly added stocks were numerous and small. The same
holds for NASDAQ in December 1972, when more than half of the stocks in the
sample but only about
`{python} f"{at(v_exch, 197212)['NASDAQ'] / at(v_exch, 197212)['Total']:.0%}"`
of its value were NASDAQ-listed.

Historically, the value of the CRSP universe has been NYSE value. NASDAQ's
share becomes substantial only from the 1990s and peaks during the dot-com
period, when it approaches
`{python} f"{at(v_exch, 200003)['NASDAQ'] / at(v_exch, 200003)['Total']:.0%}"`
of the total in March 2000, the month in which the sample's total real value
also peaks. AMEX and the Other group never account for a meaningful share of
market value at any point in the sample.

### Figure 7.3 — Number of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Industry

![](../output/figures/fig73_n_ind.png)

Manufacturing firms are the largest group in every month of the sample, and
in the early decades they are the majority: the book reports that their

the 1980s on, finance and services grow into the second and third largest

The December 1972 jumps in several industries are not economic events. They
are the NASDAQ coverage expansion of Figure 7.1 seen through the industry
lens: the newly added NASDAQ firms were concentrated in finance and in
firms without a usable industry code. The book reports that agriculture
jumps from 87 to 810 stocks and finance from 247 to 748 in that month. The
replication reproduces the finance count exactly, but the agriculture jump
does not appear; instead the "Missing" group jumps to

with placeholder SIC codes in the book's data vintage having since been
reset to zero, though the book gives no detail that would confirm the
mechanism. The lesson for sample-composition work is the same either way:
a break in an industry series should be checked against database coverage
before it is read as a change in the economy.

### Figure 7.4 — Value of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Industry

![](../output/figures/fig74_cap_ind.png)

Figure 7.3 counts firms, whereas Figure 7.4 weights their economic
importance by market value. On this measure manufacturing is even more
dominant than by count, and the picture is more stable: the entry of many
small NASDAQ firms in 1972 barely registers in value terms. Finance becomes
the clear second industry by value only in the 2000s, later than it does by
count, because many of the financial firms added in the 1970s and 1980s were
small.

The dot-com period is where the value and count pictures diverge most. The
transportation division, which includes communications, and the services
division, which includes software and internet firms, rise sharply in real
value through the late 1990s and give most of it back after March 2000. The
same reversal is visible in finance around 2008. These are the industry
components of the market-wide drawdowns that Section 5 examines.

# 3. Stock Returns and Excess Returns

## 3.1 Monthly Stock Returns

The monthly return is the `RET` field of CRSP's monthly stock file: the
return from the last trade of the previous month to the last trade of the
current month, including distributions. For the vast majority of stock-months
this is the return an investor would have realized, and it is used
unchanged. The exception is the month in which a stock is delisted. The last
trade price recorded in that month is not necessarily the value the investor
ends up with, because the investor is typically still holding the stock when
it leaves the exchange.

## 3.2 Delisting Adjustment

Delistings are often unexpected and leave no time to trade out of the
position, so a return series that stops at the last exchange trade would
overstate what investors earned, particularly for stocks removed for
financial distress. CRSP's delisting file records the delisting date
(`DLSTDT`), a reason code (`DLSTCD`), and, when CRSP can determine a
post-delisting value, the delisting return (`DLRET`). When `DLRET` is
missing the book follows Shumway (1997) and imputes a return from the reason
code:

| Month $t+1$ | Return used |
|---|---|
| No delisting | CRSP `RET` |
| Delisting, `DLRET` available | `DLRET` |
| Delisting, `DLRET` missing, `DLSTCD` in {500, 520, 551–573, 574, 580, 584} | −30% |
| Delisting, `DLRET` missing, other `DLSTCD` | −100% |

These are the specific delisting codes for which the book assigns a −30%
return when `DLRET` is unavailable. They are not a single category: the
list includes codes for a price below the exchange minimum, insufficient
capital or float, and bankruptcy, but also for a move to over-the-counter
trading, delisting at the company's request, liquidation, going private,
and "reason unavailable". All other codes receive −100%.

::: {.callout-important}
## Replacement, not compounding

The book "take[s] the return of the stock to be the delisting return." In a
delisting month the delisting return **replaces** the month's return; it is
not compounded with `RET` as $(1+RET)(1+DLRET)-1$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", "BAD = pl.col", "dl_dup =")
```

`BAD` is the book's list of −30% codes. For each delisting event the code
produces `dlfill`, the return that will be used in the delisting month:
`DLRET` when CRSP has one, and the imputed value otherwise. The adjusted
return is then obtained by taking `dlfill` where it exists and `RET`
elsewhere, which is the `coalesce` in the next code block. The filter on
`DLSTCD` is an implementation choice, not a Chapter 7 rule: CRSP's codes in
the 100s denote securities that are still active rather than delisted.

## 3.3 Excess Returns and Timing

Four return variables are used in Tables 7.2 and 7.3. With $RF_{t+1}$ the
monthly return on the risk-free security from Kenneth French's data library,

$$
\begin{aligned}
RET_{i,t+1} &: \text{CRSP } RET \text{, unadjusted} &
ret_{i,t+1} &= RET_{i,t+1} - RF_{t+1} \\
R_{i,t+1}   &: \text{delisting-adjusted return} &
r_{i,t+1}   &= R_{i,t+1} - RF_{t+1}
\end{aligned}
$$

all recorded in percent. The timing is the one described in Section 1.1:

```text
end of month t          sample membership; predictive variables measured here
        ↓
month t+1               the stock's return, R_{i,t+1}, and excess return, r_{i,t+1}
```

Within one month's cross section the same $RF_{t+1}$ is subtracted from
every stock, so raw and excess returns rank stocks identically and any
cross-sectional pattern in one is a pattern in the other. The distinction
matters in the time series: the risk-free rate varies over time, and a factor
regression of returns rather than excess returns would let that variation
contaminate the intercept. Since the intercept of such regressions is
usually the object of interest, the book works with excess returns
throughout, and $r_{i,t+1}$ is the focal return variable of Part II.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", "panel = (", "panel.write_parquet")
```

Each stock-month of the sample at $t$ is given the key of the following
month and joined *left* to the return, delisting, and risk-free tables at
$t+1$. The left join is what keeps the delisting adjustment meaningful: a
stock that is in the sample at the end of $t$ and delists during $t+1$ stays
in the cross section with its delisting return, whereas an inner join on the
stocks alive at $t+1$ would silently remove exactly the observations that
Shumway's adjustment exists to keep.

---

# 4. Return Distribution

Tables 7.2 and 7.3 summarize the cross-sectional distribution of the four
return variables with the same two-step procedure used for the annual
sample in Chapter 2, applied here month by month. Step 1 computes, for
every month $t$, the mean, standard deviation, skewness, excess kurtosis,
minimum, 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles, maximum, and number of
stocks with a valid value. Step 2 averages each of these monthly statistics
over time. The reported $n$ is therefore the average number of stocks per
month, and every other entry is the time-series mean of a cross-sectional
statistic, not a statistic of the pooled panel.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", "def xsec_m", "BOOK72 =")
```

`xsec_m()` is Step 1 for one variable and `summary()` runs it for the four
variables over a range of sample months and takes the Step 2 average. The
only difference from Chapter 2 is the frequency: the unit of the cross
section is the month rather than the year, and there are 1,038 of them.

## 4.1 Table 7.2 — Summary Statistics for Returns, 1926–2012

Sample months $t$ run from June 1926 through November 2012, the return
months $t+1$ from July 1926, the first month for which the risk-free rate is
available, through December 2012, the last month in the CRSP file.

```{python}
#| echo: false
r2(t72)
```

Selected statistics for the adjusted excess return $r_{i,t+1}$ next to the
book's values:

```{python}
#| echo: false
def cmp_row(rep, book, var, cols):
    a = rep.filter(pl.col("var") == var).row(0, named=True)
    b = book.filter(pl.col("var") == var).row(0, named=True)
    return pl.DataFrame({"Statistic": cols, "Book": [float(b[c]) for c in cols],
                         "Replication": [float(a[c]) for c in cols]}
                        ).with_columns(Difference=pl.col("Replication") - pl.col("Book"))

r2(cmp_row(t72, t72_book, "r", ["Mean", "SD", "Skew", "Kurt", "Min", "Median", "Max", "n"]))
```

Three features of the distribution carry over to everything that follows.

**Positive skewness.** In the average month the mean excess return is
positive while the median is slightly negative, and the cross-sectional
skewness is strongly positive. The asymmetry is structural: a stock cannot
lose more than 100%, so the excess return is bounded below by roughly
$-100\% - RF$, but there is no corresponding bound above. A typical stock
earns a little less than the risk-free rate in a typical month; the
positive mean comes from a minority of large winners.

**Fat tails.** The average excess kurtosis is far above the value of zero
that a normal distribution would give. The monthly cross section routinely
contains returns of several hundred percent and of close to −100%, and the
5th and 95th percentiles sit at roughly ±20%. Any method that assumes normal
returns, or that is sensitive to extreme values, has to contend with this.

**Effect of the delisting adjustment.** The adjusted and unadjusted
distributions are similar in the middle: percentiles from the 5th to the
95th differ by hundredths of a percent. The adjustment acts in the tails.
It lowers the mean slightly by adding many returns of −30% and −100%, makes
the average minimum more negative, and, because some delisting returns are
very large, raises the average maximum and with it the standard deviation
and kurtosis. The book concludes that the choice rarely changes empirical
results, but uses the adjusted return because it is closer to what an
investor realizes.

In the replication the unadjusted rows ($ret$, $RET$) reproduce the book to
the second decimal on almost every statistic, and the adjusted rows
reproduce the mean and every percentile from the 5th to the 95th. The
adjusted standard deviation, kurtosis, and maximum are lower than the
book's. The discrepancy is thus concentrated in the delisting-adjusted tail
statistics, and since the adjusted and unadjusted rows differ only in the
delisting returns, delisting-return observations are the likely source.
Confirming whether this reflects CRSP data-vintage revisions would require
a record-level comparison with the book's data vintage.

## 4.2 Table 7.3 — Summary Statistics for Returns, 1963–2012

Most empirical work does not use the full CRSP history. AMEX stocks enter
the database in July 1962, and many of the predictive variables studied in
Part II require one year of prior data, so June 1963 is the first month in
which those variables exist for AMEX stocks. The book, and the rest of Part
II, therefore uses sample months $t$ from June 1963 through November 2012,
with return months from July 1963 through December 2012. Table 7.3 repeats
Table 7.2 on that sample.

```{python}
#| echo: false
r2(t73)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
def two_samples(var, cols):
    a = t72.filter(pl.col("var") == var).row(0, named=True)
    b = t73.filter(pl.col("var") == var).row(0, named=True)
    return pl.DataFrame({"Statistic": cols, "1926–2012": [float(a[c]) for c in cols],
                         "1963–2012": [float(b[c]) for c in cols]})

print("Adjusted excess return r, replication")
r2(two_samples("r", ["Mean", "SD", "Skew", "Kurt", "Min", "Median", "Max", "n"]))
```

The post-1963 sample is a different universe rather than a shorter one. It
contains on average about half again as many stocks per month, because the
years with only NYSE coverage are gone and AMEX and NASDAQ stocks are
present throughout. The inclusion of AMEX and NASDAQ materially changes the
cross-sectional return distribution, which becomes wider and more
heavy-tailed: the cross-sectional standard deviation, the skewness, the
excess kurtosis, and the average maximum are all higher, and the average
minimum is closer to −100%. The average excess return is somewhat lower and
the median more negative. The distribution that later chapters work with is
thus wider and heavier-tailed than the full-history one.

The comparison with the book follows the pattern of Table 7.2: unadjusted
statistics match to the second decimal, adjusted percentiles and means
match, and the adjusted dispersion measures are somewhat lower in the
current data.

# 5. The Market Factor

## 5.1 Market Portfolio Proxy

In the CAPM the market portfolio is the value-weighted portfolio of *all*
assets: stocks and bonds, but also real estate, private businesses, and
human capital. That portfolio cannot be observed, and even the portfolio of
all financial securities is beyond reach because many securities have no
observable price. Empirical work therefore uses a proxy built from the
securities traded on U.S. stock exchanges, whose prices are recorded every
day.

The book compares two such proxies. The first is the value-weighted
portfolio of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP, that is, of the sample defined
in Section 1; its excess return is the Fama–French market factor, $MKT$.
The second is the broader CRSP value-weighted index, which also contains
securities that are not U.S. common stocks (foreign-incorporated firms,
closed-end funds, and other share types) but excludes ADRs. Over July 1926
to December 2012 the two excess-return series have nearly identical means
and standard deviations and a correlation of about 0.9995. The choice
between them is immaterial, and the book uses $MKT$ as the market proxy for
the remainder of the text.

## 5.2 Long-Run Market Performance

```{python}
#| echo: false
mu, sd = mkt["mkt"].mean() * 100, mkt["mkt"].std() * 100
lr = (1 + mkt["mkt"]).log()
bench = pl.DataFrame({
    "Statistic": ["Mean monthly excess return (%)", "Monthly standard deviation (%)",
                  "Annualized Sharpe ratio", "Compounded excess return, Jul 1926 – Dec 2012 (%)",
                  "Cumulative log excess return (%)"],
    "Book": [0.627, 5.43, 0.400, 14209.0, 496.0],
    "Replication": [mu, sd, mu / sd * 12 ** 0.5, mkt["compound_excess"][-1], mkt["cumulative_log_excess"][-1]],
}).with_columns(Difference=pl.col("Replication") - pl.col("Book"))
bench.with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(3))
```

The annualized Sharpe ratio is the monthly mean over the monthly standard
deviation times $\sqrt{12}$, which assumes independent monthly returns. A
premium of roughly 0.6% per month with a standard deviation of over 5% is a
noisy reward: the market's excess return in a single month is far more
likely to be dominated by risk than by the premium, and the premium reveals
itself only through compounding over decades.

## 5.3 Figure 7.5 — Cumulative Excess Returns of MKT

$$
\text{Compounded excess return}_t = 100 \times \Bigl[\prod_{s \le t}(1 + MKT_s) - 1\Bigr],
\qquad
\text{Cumulative log excess return}_t = 100 \times \sum_{s \le t} \ln(1 + MKT_s).
$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
code("ch07.py", "mkt = (", 'mkt.select("date"')
```

The compounded series is the cumulative product of one plus the monthly
market excess return, expressed as a percentage gain; the log series is the
running sum of the log of one plus the monthly excess return. `wealth` is
the cumulative product itself and is reused below for the drawdown
calculation.

![](../output/figures/fig75_mkt_cumulative.png)

The two series contain the same information, plotted on scales that answer
different questions. The compounded series gives the level: the compounded
excess-return index grows to about
`{python} f"{1 + mkt['compound_excess'][-1] / 100:.0f}"` times its initial
level by December 2012, corresponding to a cumulative excess return of about
`{python} f"{mkt['compound_excess'][-1]:,.0f}%"`. But because that number
is a level, equal percentage moves are drawn as ever larger vertical
distances as the index grows, so the
solid line makes the late sample look far more volatile than the early one
and makes the 1929–1932 crash, the largest percentage loss in the sample,
almost invisible. The log series removes that distortion: a 10% loss is the
same vertical distance in 1930 as in 2008, which is why the dashed line
shows the early crash as the deep trough it was.

### Major Drawdowns

```{python}
#| echo: false
m = mkt.with_columns(w=(1 + pl.col("mkt")).cum_prod())

def episode(peak):
    wp = m.filter(pl.col("ym") == peak)["w"][0]
    after = m.filter(pl.col("ym") > peak)
    rec = after.filter(pl.col("w") >= wp)["ym"]
    rec_ym = rec[0] if rec.len() else None
    upto = after.filter(pl.col("ym") < rec_ym) if rec_ym else after
    trough = upto.filter(pl.col("w") == pl.col("w").min())
    return trough["ym"][0], (trough["w"][0] / wp - 1) * 100, rec_ym

def label(ym):
    return f"{ym // 100}-{ym % 100:02d}" if ym else "not by Dec 2012"

rows = []
for peak, book_dd, book_rec in [(192908, -85, "1945-04"), (196811, -56, "1983-04"),
                                 (198708, -31, "1991-05"), (200003, -54, "not by Dec 2012")]:
    t, dd, rec = episode(peak)
    rows.append((f"{label(peak)} → {label(t)}", f"about {book_dd}%", f"{dd:.1f}%", book_rec, label(rec)))
pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=["Episode (peak → trough)", "Book drawdown", "Replication",
                           "Book recovery", "Replication recovery"], orient="row")
```

Drawdowns are measured from the running high-water mark of the compounded
series; recovery is the first month in which cumulative wealth again reaches
the previous peak. The 1929 crash needed more than fifteen years to recover;
the 1968 and 2000 episodes, each more than half of cumulative wealth,
needed fourteen years and more than the twelve years remaining in the
sample, respectively. October 1987, with a monthly excess return of about
−23%, produced the smallest of the four drawdowns and the fastest recovery.

Figure 7.5 shows that a strongly positive long-run market premium can
coexist with very large and long-lasting drawdowns. The premium is real,
but an investor collects it only by holding through periods in which more
than half of accumulated wealth disappears and is not recovered for a
decade or more. In the CAPM, beta measures a stock's exposure to variation
in this market factor.

---

# Summary

Chapter 7 fixes the objects that the rest of the book takes as given. The
sample is the set of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP at each month-end,
whose composition by exchange and by industry changes materially over
1925–2012, both through real economic shifts and through discrete changes
in database coverage in 1962 and 1972. The monthly return is CRSP's `RET`
with the delisting month replaced by the delisting return or its Shumway
(1997) imputation, an adjustment that leaves the center of the
cross-sectional distribution unchanged but matters in its tails. The
one-month-ahead excess return $r_{i,t+1}$ is the focal return variable, and
its cross section is strongly right-skewed and heavy-tailed.

The market portfolio is proxied by the Fama–French $MKT$ factor, whose
long-run premium is unmistakably positive and yet is earned through
drawdowns of 50–85% lasting a decade or more. Every asset-pricing analysis
in the chapters that follow, from the CAPM risk model to the
cross-sectional regressions of Part II, is built on this sample, these
return definitions, and this market factor.
